title: Leviathan
author: Thomas Hobbes
note: The founding argument for why people submit to a common power at all. Hobbes starts from individuals in a state of nature and builds the state from their consent, which is the question any new jurisdiction has to answer for itself.

title: Second Treatise of Government
author: John Locke
note: Locke’s answer to Hobbes: government exists to protect life, liberty and property, holds power only in trust, and can be dissolved when it breaks that trust. The second of his Two Treatises, and the one later constitutions borrowed from.

title: The Federalist Papers
author: Alexander Hamilton, James Madison and John Jay
note: Eighty-five essays arguing for a new constitution, written to persuade people who could still say no. The clearest record of founders reasoning in public about factions, separation of powers and how a design fails.

title: On Liberty
author: John Stuart Mill
note: Where the line sits between what a society may decide for you and what is yours alone. Mill’s harm principle and his defence of free discussion are still the starting point for arguments about speech and moderation.

title: Civil Disobedience
author: Henry David Thoreau
note: A short essay on what a person owes a government they did not choose and do not agree with. Thoreau’s answer is to withdraw cooperation, which makes it an early text on exit as well as protest.

title: No Treason
author: Lysander Spooner
note: Spooner asks whether a constitution can bind anyone who never signed it, and concludes it cannot. The sharpest statement of the case for explicit, individual consent, which is exactly what an on-chain founding agreement claims to provide.

title: The Wealth of Nations
author: Adam Smith
note: The book that explained how specialisation and trade make a society rich without anyone directing it. Long, but Book I on the division of labour, money and prices is the part everything else in economics leans on.

title: The Republic
author: Plato, translated by Benjamin Jowett
note: The first attempt to design a just city from first principles, and to ask who should rule it. Worth reading as much for where the design goes wrong as for what it gets right.

title: Magna Carta
author: King John and the barons of England, translated by W. S. McKechnie
note: The charter in which a king accepted, in writing, that he was bound by law. Most clauses are about feudal dues; clauses 39 and 40, on lawful judgment and justice not being sold, are why it is still read.

title: The Declaration of Independence
author: Thomas Jefferson and the Second Continental Congress
note: A founding document written as an argument: what governments are for, what this one did wrong, and why separation follows. A model of how to state a case for exit plainly.

title: Bitcoin: A Peer-to-Peer Electronic Cash System
author: Satoshi Nakamoto
note: Nine pages that solved double-spending without a trusted party and started everything this network is built on. Short enough to read in one sitting and precise enough to reread.

title: The Cathedral and the Bazaar
author: Eric S. Raymond
note: Why software built in the open by loosely coordinated strangers can beat software built behind closed doors. The lessons about releasing early and treating users as co-developers apply to building a network as much as a mail client.

title: Smart Contracts
author: Nick Szabo
note: The two-page note that named the idea: agreements whose terms are carried out by protocol, so that breaking them is expensive rather than merely illegal. Written twenty years before anyone could deploy one.

title: Ethereum Whitepaper: A Next-Generation Smart Contract and Decentralized Application Platform
author: Vitalik Buterin
note: The proposal to put a general-purpose computer on a blockchain, so that contracts, organisations and currencies become programs anyone can deploy. Parts are dated (it predates proof of stake), but it is still the clearest statement of the idea this network runs on.
